title: Native Messaging framing and transport limits
description: Normative transport facts for the extension-to-host pipe, including who may speak on it (senderPolicy). Written as data because both implementations must agree on the same numbers: the Go host and the TypeScript client are tested against this file in Phase 2 (fixtures/protocol/*.jsonl replay them).

lengthPrefix.meaning: Byte length of the JSON payload that follows, UTF-8, excluding the prefix itself.

payload.note: Native Messaging is message-delimited, not byte-stream: never split or merge a JSON object across frames. A frame is a single envelope object, never an array.

extensionToHostBytes.reason: Chrome's documented cap on a message sent to the host.
extensionToHostBytes.enforcement: sender must reject before write, not the receiver after read

hostToExtensionBytes.reason: Chrome allows 1 GB host-to-extension; Firefox historically caps at 1 MB, so anything larger must be chunked for cross-browser parity (docs/architecture/25).
hostToExtensionBytes.enforcement: receiver must treat a frame larger than the effective limit as a transport error and reconnect, not truncate

alternativesRejected.option: out-of-band file handoff (extension writes a temp file, host reads it)
alternativesRejected.why_rejected: The extension cannot write arbitrary paths (no filesystem API in a service worker), and a handoff directory reintroduces the exact trust problem ADR-0004 removed: another local process could race or replace the file. Native Messaging gives an authenticated pipe; a temp file does not.

alternativesRejected.option: raise the limit by splitting the subscription through the Connector's own fetch
alternativesRejected.why_rejected: Moves subscription ownership into the Connector for a transport reason, and would make subscription refresh untestable from the extension while still not solving >1 MB requests.

mechanism.ordering: chunks of one contentHash must arrive in chunkSeq order; a gap fails the whole import with IntegrityMismatch rather than partially applying
mechanism.atomicity: reassembly completes, hashes, validates, and only then replaces the previous good set (validate-then-apply)
mechanism.cap: total reassembled bytes bounded by subscription-source limits.maxBytes

liveness.note: Chrome tears out the port when the extension's service worker is evicted. The Connector and Core MUST survive that (ADR-0005) -- a dropped port is a client reconnect event, never a shutdown signal.

reconnect.afterReconnect: re-run connector.hello, then reconcile: the extension sends config.snapshot hash and the Connector answers whether the applied config still matches.

ordering.rule: Frames on one port are delivered in order per sender. Cross-sender ordering is not assumed; seq is assigned by each sender and only used for gap detection.
ordering.backpressure: Sender stops issuing requests beyond limits.maxConcurrentRequests; there is no unbounded queue in either direction.

nonGoals: no streaming of large bodies inside one logical message beyond chunk envelopes
no secrets inside traceId or event names
no protocol defined by NEXORA over the network -- the pipe is local and its only job is control (ADR-0004)

senderPolicy.description: Who may speak on this pipe, how often, and what a refusal costs. This lives next to the byte limits because it is the same class of fact: a transport property both implementations must agree on, not a product preference. The numbers are budgets a UI defect can exhaust, not a rate the user is expected to notice.

identity.resolvedFrom: the Native Messaging manifest registration the OS hands the host when the port opens -- the extension cannot choose it and the caller cannot claim it (ADR-0004 rule 3)
notIdentity: a payload field asserting that the caller is the extension
the method name or its args
identity.allowlistSource: the host's own startup configuration on disk, written by the Connector installer
identity.allowlistNeverIn: browser storage: -nexora.settings is written through the code path rule 6 exists to constrain, so letting the caller configure its own authorization is not a control
identity.unknownSender: answer UnauthorizedExtension and do not touch state (ADR-0004 rule 6)

privilegedMethods.declaredIn: protocol/command-allowlist.json -- the commands[].privileged flag, not a name pattern
privilegedMethods.rule: a Connector build MAY refuse these to a sender that is not the pinned extension id (docs/architecture/26 section 2, docs/architecture/31 section 5); a refusal is UnauthorizedExtension with no state change
privilegedMethods.why: every one of them starts a process, writes the keystore, deletes an entity, or emits traffic the user did not type -- so they are the methods a compromised or buggy UI can do damage with

rateLimits.why: args.force bypasses the per-source backoff (subscription-source status.nextAttemptAt) and this budget is the only thing left between a stuck options tab and the user's feed provider; one call may carry forty sources, so the budget counts calls, not fetches
enough for a 'test all' on one panel of servers, too small for a poll loop to reach every VPS on the user's list every second; probes are never retried, so a refusal is not a lost measurement
each may restart Core, and a restart drops every live tunnel: a state-change storm is a self-inflicted outage, and converge-to-desired-state means the user loses nothing by being asked to wait
replace-class and destructive: a second import inside a minute is either a retry of the first (idempotency answers it) or a bug, and keystore.purge cannot be un-done
it reads logs and writes a dump to disk, so it is the most expensive read on the pipe; a UI that polls diagnostics is asking for a file the user has to delete
the floor every other row sits under: it bounds the pipe itself against a spinning worker, so a budget mistake in one row cannot turn into an unbounded queue

rateLimitFacts.scopeOfBudget: per sender id, per Connector process, not per browser tab -- the Connector is single-instance by design (ADR-0005)
rateLimitFacts.notPersisted: spent budget dies with the process; a reconnect is not a fresh budget for an attacker but is for a user who restarted the browser
rateLimitFacts.refusalIsRetryable: onExceed is always Busy, whose taxonomy entry declares retryable true; QuotaExceeded is a storage-layer code and must never be the answer to a rate limit, because a client cannot tell 'back off' from 'you are out of space'
rateLimitFacts.countedWhere: the Connector, before it hands the frame to a handler: a request refused by budget never reaches the handler, so it cannot half-apply. Never the shim -- a scoped budget names a method, and the method name is inside the payload, which `docs/architecture/25-native-messaging-protocol.md` §2 forbids the shim to interpret. What the shim does enforce is what an opened port and a frame header answer without opening the payload: the sender allowlist, the byte limits, and the ports per sender

refusals.loggedFields: sender id, method name, window remaining -- never args, which may carry a document the user typed (docs/architecture/32)

amplificationGuard.then: close the port rather than keep answering
amplificationGuard.why: an unallowlisted sender with a retry loop is a CPU and log-volume attack on the only process that holds the keystore; closing the pipe is the response that costs the attacker nothing to notice and the host nothing to compute

portsPerSender.why: MV3 eviction legitimately overlaps an old port with a reconnect; three or more means either a leak the extension should fix or a second registration, and the Connector has no reason to serve both
